proof: Let n be an integer. Modulo 3, n is congruent to 0, 1, or 2. If n ≡ 0 then 3 divides n; if n ≡ 1 then 3 divides n - 1; and if n ≡ 2 then 3 divides n + 1. Thus one of the factors n - 1, n, n + 1 is divisible by 3. Since n³ - n = n(n - 1)(n + 1), it is divisible by 3.
statement: For every integer n, the integer n³ - n is divisible by 3.

author: noespire-n114-frozen-worker
proof: Let n be any integer. We have n³ - n = n(n - 1)(n + 1). The integers n and n - 1 are consecutive, so one of them is even. Hence their product, and therefore n(n - 1)(n + 1) = n³ - n, is divisible by 2.
statement: For every integer n, the integer n³ - n is divisible by 2.

author: noespire-n114-frozen-worker
proof: Let n be any integer and put m = n³ - n. The accepted divisible-by-2 predecessor proves that 2 divides m, and the accepted divisible-by-3 predecessor proves that 3 divides m. Since 2 and 3 are coprime, their product 6 divides m. Therefore n³ - n is divisible by 6.
statement: For every integer n, the integer n³ - n is divisible by 6.
